title: Verizon Security Services
industry_source_label: local telephone provider entering home security
concepts_tested: cost-structure assessment for a new business line
prompt: Verizon is the nation's largest provider of local telephone services. They are considering entering the home security market. Should they?

clarifying_info.answer: No hard data is given — candidate must set assumptions. Sample: Total US households 100M; % serviceable by Verizon 50%; % of households that can afford service 50%; annual subscription price $250 → Total Addressable Market = 100M × 50% × 50% × $250 = $6.25B.

Very little fixed cost beyond infrastructure already in customers' homes (existing phone wiring). Door/window/motion sensors can be installed by a third-party installer, billed to the customer at cost + markup, and owned by the customer. Variable costs are also small — mainly enough call-center operators to dispatch police when alarms trip. Verizon has little cost advantage over other players (all use the common carrier phone network), though it may get slight call-center scale economies.
Fragmented market of mostly mom-and-pop alarm operators; no firm has over 5% market share overall, though some strong regional players exist.

Candidate should speculate on segments; a reasonable split is urban vs. suburban (assume 50/50). Urban customers likely have lower income but higher willingness to pay due to higher crime rates; suburban customers likely have higher income but lower perceived threat. First-degree price discrimination could justify charging suburban customers a higher price since they're less price sensitive.

No fixed answer, but candidate must justify their pricing logic — e.g., insurance companies give homeowner's-insurance discounts for alarms (raises perceived value); comparison to other monthly services (cable, phone, DSL); need to stay competitive with existing players; could instead assume a net margin off market size rather than set an end-consumer price.
The market is not regulated, and government regulation is not expected to play a role.

Verizon has monthly contact with a large pool of potential customers via phone bills; it already has brand loyalty for phone service; its size and deep pockets enable marketing scale economies and broad reach.

interviewer_notes: This is a broad, qualitative strategy case given in an open and conversational manner — no hard data is provided. Make the candidate come up with his/her own assumptions and estimates for everything; there is no single 'right' answer, but the candidate must reach reasonable assumptions and follow them logically to a conclusion. Use the sample assumptions provided to steer the candidate back on track if they go off the reservation.

suggested_framework.summary: Evaluate the home-security market-entry decision across market size/attractiveness, cost structure, competitive landscape, customer segments and pricing, and Verizon's unique capabilities (brand, customer reach, scale).

tree.label: Should Verizon enter the home security market?

stages.interviewer_asks: Verizon is considering entering the home security market. How would you think about whether they should?
stages.expected_answer: Candidate lays out an open-ended framework covering market size/attractiveness, cost structure, competitive landscape, customer segments and pricing, and Verizon's specific right to win, and states they will build assumptions to work through each.
good_answer_signals: Proposes a structure before diving into numbers
Signals willingness to make and state explicit assumptions since no hard data will be given

stages.interviewer_asks: How big is the home security market opportunity for Verizon?
stages.release_when: Only if candidate asks for market size; have them set their own assumptions first
stages.info_to_release: Sample assumptions to steer them if needed: 100M US households; 50% serviceable by Verizon; 50% can afford the service; $250 annual subscription price.
stages.expected_answer: Candidate proposes reasonable assumptions and computes a total addressable market; sample calculation: 100M × 50% × 50% × $250 = $6.25B.
good_answer_signals: Arrives at a reasonable order-of-magnitude TAM

stages.interviewer_asks: What would the cost structure look like for Verizon to enter this market? What are the fixed costs? Variable costs? Does Verizon have a cost advantage?
stages.expected_answer: Fixed costs are minimal (existing home phone wiring reused; sensors installed and owned by the customer, billed by a third party at cost + markup). Variable costs are small — mainly call-center staff to dispatch police on alarm trips. Verizon has little inherent cost advantage since all players use the common carrier network, aside from a slight call-center scale benefit.
good_answer_signals: Separates fixed vs. variable cost clearly
Recognizes the business can piggyback on existing phone infrastructure
Correctly judges the cost advantage as minor, not decisive

stages.interviewer_asks: What does the competitive landscape look like?
stages.info_to_release: Fragmented market of mom-and-pop alarm operators; no firm has over 5% share, though some strong regional players exist.
stages.expected_answer: The market is highly fragmented with no dominant national player, which is favorable for a large, well-resourced new entrant like Verizon.
good_answer_signals: Notes the fragmentation as an opportunity for a scaled entrant

stages.interviewer_asks: What customer segments would you expect, and how important/sizable/valuable is each?
stages.expected_answer: A reasonable segmentation is urban vs. suburban customers (assume ~50/50). Urban customers likely have lower income but higher willingness to pay due to higher crime rates; suburban customers likely have higher income but lower perceived threat, supporting first-degree price discrimination (charge suburban customers more since they're less price sensitive).
good_answer_signals: Connects segment characteristics to differentiated willingness to pay

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you price the service for each segment?
stages.expected_answer: No single right answer, but candidate should justify the pricing logic — e.g., leveraging insurance discounts on alarm-equipped homes, benchmarking against other monthly household services (cable, phone, DSL), staying competitive with incumbents, or instead assuming a net margin against market size rather than deriving an end-consumer price.
good_answer_signals: Grounds pricing in a clear rationale rather than picking an arbitrary number
Considers at least one benchmark (insurance, comparable services, competitor pricing)

stages.interviewer_asks: Is there any regulatory consideration here?
stages.info_to_release: The market is unregulated and regulation is not expected to become a factor.
stages.expected_answer: Candidate notes regulation is a minor/non-issue in this market.
good_answer_signals: Doesn't overweight regulation given the information provided

stages.interviewer_asks: What advantages might Verizon have in marketing this new service versus its competitors?
stages.expected_answer: Verizon has monthly touchpoints with a huge customer base via its phone bill; it has existing brand loyalty/trust for phone service that could extend to alarm service; and its size and deep pockets give it marketing scale economies that small regional competitors lack.

stages.interviewer_asks: [With ~3 minutes left] So, should Verizon enter into the home security market?
stages.expected_answer: Yes. Verizon has several meaningful advantages: call-center scale economies keep it cost-competitive, an established brand associated with reliability and networking/communications, and — most importantly — monthly contact with ~50M households via its phone bill that it can use to launch and market the new service, plus deep pockets to out-advertise small regional competitors. On a market of roughly $6B in Verizon's territory, even a 10% share would add about $600M in revenue, and given the low cost structure and high perceived customer value, this is likely to be highly profitable revenue. Verizon should be able to become the national leader in this space.
good_answer_signals: Gives an unprompted, clear recommendation as time runs low
Ties the recommendation back to Verizon's specific advantages, not just general market attractiveness

math.question: What is a reasonable total addressable market (TAM) for home security service in Verizon's territory?
givens: % of households that can afford the service: 50%
math.answer: $6.25B total addressable market (sample assumptions; no single right answer)

math.question: If Verizon captures 10% share of a ~$6B addressable market, how much revenue would that add?

synthesis: Yes, Verizon should enter the home security market. It has real, if modest, competitive advantages — call-center scale economies, a trusted communications/reliability brand, and above all direct monthly contact with roughly 50M households via its phone bill, which it can use to market the new service cheaply and broadly. On a market sized at roughly $6B in its territory, even a 10% share would add about $600M in revenue, and given the low cost structure and high perceived customer value, that revenue is likely to be highly profitable. With its marketing reach and financial resources, Verizon should be able to capture significant share and become the national leader in home security.
what_great_looks_like: Proposes and states explicit, reasonable assumptions rather than waiting for data, since the case is deliberately open-ended
Builds a sensible market-sizing calculation and sanity-checks the order of magnitude
Separates fixed and variable costs and correctly judges that Verizon's cost advantage is modest
Identifies Verizon's unique assets (existing customer base, brand, scale) rather than generic market-entry logic
Reaches a clear, well-justified recommendation without prompting as time runs low
common_pitfalls: Waits for the interviewer to supply data instead of proposing assumptions, given the case's explicitly open-ended format
Treats this as a generic new-market-entry case without identifying what specifically makes Verizon a strong entrant (existing billing relationship, brand, scale)
Overweights cost advantage as a differentiator when the case indicates it is minor
Skips justifying the pricing scheme with any rationale

extraction.notes: The book's sample TAM ($6.25B) and its conclusion's rounded market size ($6B) are consistent (the conclusion's $6B is a rounded restatement of the $6.25B sample TAM, both already scoped to 'Verizon's territory'); no discrepancy found.
